Selfsame
SELF-same
adj.
From self and same, an intensive compound meaning the very same and no other. Webster 1828: the very same; identical. The Authorized Version uses it where exactness matters — the day of the Exodus, the Spirit who distributes gifts, and the God who prepared the believer for glory.

Biblical Definition

Selfsame is the Authorized Version’s emphatic the very same, and it appears where the text insists on precision. The Exodus is dated to the day: at the end of the four hundred and thirty years, even the selfsame day it came to pass, that all the hosts of the LORD went out from the land of Egypt (Exodus 12:41). Not approximately, not in that season — the selfsame day. God keeps a calendar. Paul uses it of the distribution of gifts in the church: all these worketh that one and the selfsame Spirit, dividing to every man severally as he will (1 Corinthians 12:11). The diversity of gifts is real and it is not evidence of different sources or different degrees of spirituality; one Spirit apportions, and He apportions as He wills, not as the recipient chooses. And in 2 Corinthians the word carries the doctrine of glorification: having spoken of the earthly house of this tabernacle being dissolved and of the building of God eternal in the heavens, Paul writes, Now he that hath wrought us for the selfsame thing is God, who also hath given unto us the earnest of the Spirit (2 Corinthians 5:5). The believer was made for that very thing; the Spirit is the down payment; and God is the one who did the making.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines SELFSAME as the very same; identical, and marks it as an intensive of same. The compound is now archaic in ordinary speech but was standard in the English of 1611 and still current in 1828.

expand to see more

SELFSAME, a. — The very same; identical.

The compound is intensive: same alone might admit of a likeness, while selfsame asserts identity.

The Authorized Version uses it some fifteen times, chiefly in Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Ezekiel, and the Pauline epistles.

In the selfsame day is a legal and chronological formula in the Pentateuch (Genesis 7:13; 17:23, 26; Exodus 12:17, 41, 51).

Its persistence in modern English is almost entirely due to the King James Version.

Key Scripture

Exodus 12:41 — "And it came to pass at the end of the four hundred and thirty years, even the selfsame day it came to pass, that all the hosts of the LORD went out from the land of Egypt."

1 Corinthians 12:11 — "But all these worketh that one and the selfsame Spirit, dividing to every man severally as he will."

2 Corinthians 5:5 — "Now he that hath wrought us for the selfsame thing is God, who also hath given unto us the earnest of the Spirit."

Genesis 7:13 — "In the selfsame day entered Noah, and Shem, and Ham, and Japheth, the sons of Noah, and Noah’s wife, and the three wives of his sons with them, into the ark;"

Galatians 4:4 — "But when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law,"

Modern Corruption

1 Corinthians 12:11 is the verse that settles the modern quarrel about gifts, and both sides of it need the correction: the Spirit divides as he will, which rules out both the demand for a particular gift and the contempt for those who lack one.

expand to see more

The charismatic error presses believers toward a specific gift as the mark of a fuller Christianity, and Paul’s whole chapter is written against exactly that at Corinth. He asks a series of questions expecting the answer no — are all apostles? are all prophets?… do all speak with tongues? — and grounds the diversity in the Spirit’s sovereign distribution: dividing to every man severally as he will. The cessationist must hear the same verse from his side: the sovereignty asserted is the Spirit’s, not the church’s, and contempt for a member because of the gift he has or lacks is the precise sin of the foot saying it is not of the body. The chapter’s aim is that there be no schism in the body, and it ends by pointing to a more excellent way.

The chronological uses of the word deserve their own note, because they show a God who keeps dates. Noah entered the ark in the selfsame day; Abraham was circumcised in the selfsame day; Israel came out of Egypt on the selfsame day at the end of four hundred and thirty years. Paul’s when the fulness of the time was come is the same doctrine applied to the incarnation. The believer who has been waiting years for an answer is dealing with the God of the selfsame day, and 2 Corinthians 5:5 tells him what he was made for: not merely to be delivered, but to be clothed upon with a house from heaven, and the Spirit already in him is the earnest of it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew etsem (H6106), a bone, and by extension the substance or self of a thing — be’etsem hayyom hazzeh, in the bone of this day, is the idiom for the selfsame day; Greek autos (G846), the same.

expand to see more

Hebrew etsem (H6106) — a bone; and figuratively the substance or very self of a thing.

Hebrew be’etsem hayyom hazzeh — literally in the bone of this day, the idiom rendered in the selfsame day.

Greek autos (G846) — self, same; one and the selfsame Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:11).

Greek arrabon (G728) — an earnest, a pledge or down payment; 2 Corinthians 5:5, Ephesians 1:14.

Greek katergazomai (G2716) — to work out, to accomplish thoroughly; he that hath wrought us for the selfsame thing.

Usage

"Even the selfsame day… the hosts of the LORD went out (Exodus 12:41) — God keeping a four-hundred-year appointment."

"That one and the selfsame Spirit, dividing to every man severally as he will (1 Corinthians 12:11) — sovereign distribution."

"He that hath wrought us for the selfsame thing is God (2 Corinthians 5:5) — the believer made for glory."
